doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

chapter: Teaching and spread of New Orleans jazz
title: Why music schools fluff off early jazz and why it is hard to teach
summary: White says teachers only know classical and modern jazz; Rowe notes the music resists codifying, and White asks how to teach soulful collective improvisation.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Oh to finish the question, most music teachers are only taught classical music and modern jazz. And so they fluff over early jazz as something invalid. Now if I only had to hear what is all over the country as the Dixieland that I’ve heard, I wouldn’t have liked it and wouldn’t have gotten into it either. But you know, so they put that label on early jazz music and they think that’s what it is and that’s how it sounds and all of that. And so no, I mean a lot of music schools – it’s partly because a lot of music teachers, what I find is they don’t know about it, they don’t want to know about it, they don’t understand it, so they just kind of fluff it off as invalid. You know, learn all these bebop scales and imitate Charlie Parker and John Coltrane and that’s real jazz you know.

I think you started to answer my question because I think it’s probably harder to teach this music. Because try to think of the last time you saw a New Orleans style jazz group play with music stands in front of them. And I don’t think the music lends itself to being codified, to have all those scales and it’s such a personal thing, and all those connections, those community connections you just mentioned that are part and the reason for the music. How do you teach that? And if someone can’t teach it they decide well maybe it’s not worth teaching.
